---
title: "Remote LCD Display"
unit: 3
cluster: "Controlling the Board Remotely"
---

In the previous lesson, we've seen how to start a server on a esp32 board and receive messages. In this lesson, lets try to make a LCD display that could be controlled remotely.

## What the board needs

The board needs these files saved on it:

- `lcd_api.py` and `machine_i2c_lcd.py`, from [Saving a Module on the Board](../display/saving-a-module-on-the-board.qmd)
- `wifi.py`, from [Connecting to Wi-Fi](../internet/connecting-to-wifi.qmd)
- `server.py`, from [Starting a Server on the Board](starting-a-server-on-the-board.qmd)

Connect the display as in [Showing Text on an LCD](../display/showing-text-on-an-lcd.qmd): SDA to GPIO4 and SCL to
GPIO5.

## The program on the board

```python
from machine import I2C, Pin
from machine_i2c_lcd import I2cLcd
import time
import server
import wifi

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=100000)
lcd = I2cLcd(i2c, 39, 2, 16)

def show(message):
    lcd.clear()
    lcd.putstr(message)
    return "showing " + message

lcd.clear()
lcd.putstr("Connecting...")

# Use your wifi network name and password in the next line
ip = wifi.connect("MyPhone", "mypassword")
print("Board address:", ip)

# Show the address on the display, so the laptop can find the board
lcd.clear()
if ip is None:
    lcd.putstr("No Wi-Fi")
else:
    lcd.putstr(ip)

server.start(5000)
print("Waiting on port 5000")

while True:
    messages = server.receive()
    for client_address, line in messages:
        print(client_address[0], "sent", line)
        response = show(line)
        server.reply(client_address, response)

    time.sleep(0.01)
```

Click Run. The display shows `Connecting...` while the board joins the
Wi-Fi, and then its address:

```text
192.168.43.57
```

The address will be different in your case. Once the board shows it on the
display, you don't need Thonny's Shell to find it.

`show()` replies with what it showed, so the laptop sees the message the
board got.

## The program on the laptop

::: {.callout-important}
This program runs on the **laptop**, not on the board.
:::

On the laptop, keep a copy of `server.py` in the same directory as the
program, as in [Starting a Server on the Board](starting-a-server-on-the-board.qmd). Save this program next to it
as `remote_lcd.py`, with your board's address:

```python
import sys
import server

server_address = ("192.168.43.57", 5000)

message = sys.argv[1]
response = server.send(server_address, message)
if response is not None:
    print(response)
```

The message is the program's first command-line argument. If the board does
not reply, `server.send()` prints why, and returns `None`, so the program
prints nothing more.

## Sending a message

In the terminal on the laptop, put the message in double quotes, so the
shell passes it to the program as one argument:

```session
$ python3 remote_lcd.py "Class at 2 pm"
showing Class at 2 pm
```

The display shows `Class at 2 pm` straight away.

Without the quotes, each word is a separate argument, and the program sends
only the first one, `Class`.

The display has 2 lines of 16 characters. A message longer than 16
characters goes on to the second line. Keep it to 32.

Any command's output can be the message, with `$(...)`. Show the time on
the laptop:

```session
$ python3 remote_lcd.py "$(date +%H:%M)"
showing 14:05
```

## Summary

A server on the board can show each message it receives on the display,
and a program on the laptop can send it a message given on the command
line.
